name: Uvinul A Plus

lead: Uvinul A Plus is a photostable UVA filter found in EU sunscreens, chosen by people who want strong UVA protection against skin aging and pigmentation. Absorbing UVA means less photoaging and fewer dark spots over time.

It is also known as diethylamino hydroxybenzoyl hexyl benzoate (DHHB, Parsol DHHB), absorbs UVA with a peak near 354 nm, and is used in the EU at up to 10 percent. Published material covers chemistry and a 2020 human metabolism study rather than appearance outcomes.

paras: People look for DHHB on ingredient lists of European sunscreens and daily facial products, usually combined with other filters, and apply it as an everyday morning step. It is not a US sunscreen active.
The EU safety committee flagged a manufacturing impurity (di-n-hexyl phthalate) and recommended limits. Human metabolism was studied after oral and dermal doses in 2020.

angle.text: Uvinul A Plus is a photostable UVA filter found in EU sunscreens, sought by users who want strong UVA protection against skin aging and pigmentation. Absorbing UVA means less photoaging and fewer dark spots over time.

lead: Uvinul A Plus is BASF's trade name for diethylamino hydroxybenzoyl hexyl benzoate (DHHB, also sold as Parsol DHHB by DSM), an organic UVA-absorbing sunscreen filter. It is used in sunscreens and other cosmetics in the European Union at up to 10 percent, and is described as photostable [1][2][3].

It helps appearance through photoaging protection. UVA penetrates deeper into skin than UVB and causes little visible reddening, and Wikipedia's sunscreen article says sunlight is a major driver of premature aging and that daily broad-spectrum sunscreen use has been associated with smoother, more resilient skin [4]. A UVA filter such as DHHB is one way formulators build the UVA side of broad-spectrum protection into a sunscreen [3][4].

Published research on the filter itself is chemical and toxicokinetic: a 2017 photophysics study, a 2020 human metabolism study, a 2019 urinary biomonitoring method, a 2021 water-degradation study and a 2025 metabolite study [1][2][5][6][7]. No trials of appearance outcomes for this filter alone were found.

paras: DHHB is mainly used in sunscreens, and also appears in other cosmetic products, with a maximum concentration of 10 percent under the EU directive [1][5]. Wikipedia's sunscreen article notes that the EU approves more UV filters than the US because the US treats sunscreen as an over-the-counter drug while the EU treats it as a cosmetic; it counts 29 filters approved in the EU against 17 in the US as of 2023 [4].

The compound is described as compatible with other UV absorbers and cosmetic ingredients, which is part of why it is combined with UVB filters in broad-spectrum formulas [3]. In the EU, a product must reach a UVA protection factor of at least one-third of its SPF and a critical wavelength of at least 370 nm to carry the UVA seal, a standard that UVA filters help products meet [4].

DHHB is a synthetic benzophenone derivative with the preferred name hexyl 2-[4-(diethylamino)-2-hydroxybenzoyl]benzoate [5][3]. It is made by reacting 3-hydroxy-N,N-diethylaniline with phthalic anhydride and then esterifying the product with 1-hexanol [3].

A 2017 photophysical study examined DHHB through transient absorption, emission, phosphorescence and electron paramagnetic resonance spectra, describing it as a photostable UVA absorber [2]. Wikipedia lists a maximum absorbance of 354 nm [3]. A 2021 water-chemistry study found only about 15 percent degradation after six hours of artificial irradiation, describing the filter as extremely photostable [6]. Wikipedia's sunscreen article says most organic UV filters do not break down significantly in sunlight, with avobenzone the notable exception that needs stabilisers [4].
Wikipedia states that the EU approved DHHB for sunscreens in 2005 at up to 10 percent, and that it is also approved in South America, Mexico, Japan and Taiwan but is not a US sunscreen active [3].

The EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety (SCCS) flagged possible contamination with di-n-hexyl phthalate from manufacturing and recommended a limit of 260 ppm in DHHB for sunscreens, with a target below 1 ppm because the contamination is avoidable [3]. Wikipedia describes DHHB itself as a safe sunscreen ingredient [3].

A 2020 study gave volunteers a single oral or dermal dose and followed metabolism and urinary excretion over 72 hours; three major urinary metabolites accounted for 52% of the oral dose, and the authors estimated daily systemic exposure in spot urine samples from 58 volunteers at about 8.1 to 9.3 micrograms per day, which they described as very low relative to the no observed adverse effect level [1]. A 2019 method for measuring metabolites in urine found them in about 36% of 58 samples from the general German population, and the authors noted that no information on human systemic exposure had previously been available [5].

A 2021 study found DHHB degrades quickly under drinking-water disinfection conditions, with a half-life of about 116 seconds in the tested chlorine conditions, forming mono- and dichlorinated products [6]. A 2025 study synthesised a human acyl glucuronide metabolite and tested its acute aquatic toxicity in a bioluminescence assay [7].
A 2020 human study examined metabolism and urinary excretion after single oral and dermal exposure [1]. No studies of skin-appearance or photoprotection outcomes for this filter alone were found.

Studies of sunscreen use generally, rather than of this filter, are summarised on Wikipedia: a 32-person study in which daily SPF 30 use was reported to reverse photoaging within 12 weeks, and an Australian study of about 900 people in which daily broad-spectrum use over four and a half years was associated with smoother, more resilient skin [4].

timeline.event: EU approves DHHB as a sunscreen filter at up to 10 percent [3].
Di-n-hexyl phthalate, the manufacturing impurity flagged by the SCCS, joins the ECHA list of Substances of Very High Concern, according to Wikipedia [3].
